title: Consent enforced on reads
summary: A withdrawn consent is not a flag in a spreadsheet: the next read of that person, for that purpose, is refused by the vault itself - and so is the handoff that would have carried the data out.

steps.label: The person exists and support may read them
steps.note: Registration first, so there is a record to govern. Absence of a consent row means 'not consent-governed' - the read works because nobody has withdrawn anything yet.

steps.label: Read the email for support - allowed
steps.note: The baseline: one field, one stated purpose, 200.

steps.label: The person withdraws consent for support
steps.note: One record of a decision, stored next to the data it governs. In production this call comes from the privacy portal the person used, or from the desk on their request.

steps.label: The same read is now a 403
steps.note: Nothing changed in the caller: the same client, the same credential, the same purpose. The vault refuses because the person said no. This is the difference between a policy and an enforcement point.

steps.label: And the handoff for that purpose is refused too
steps.note: Consent is checked when an identifier is minted, not only when a field is read - otherwise a system could take the data out through a token issued a second before the withdrawal took effect.

steps.label: An unrelated purpose is unaffected
steps.note: Withdrawal is per purpose, not a global switch: order fulfilment still works because that is a different lawful basis and a different decision.

steps.label: The person changes their mind
steps.note: Re-granting restores access immediately - and the decision list keeps both records, because 'when did they consent' is a question you will be asked.

steps.label: Reading works again, and the decisions are on the record
steps.note: The consent list is what an auditor asks for: which purposes, granted or withdrawn, and when.
